item.research_question: Can the stacking fault energy (SFE) be treated as a unique intrinsic property in concentrated alloys, and are dissociation distances still governed solely by SFE when the average SFE is zero or negative?
item.material_system: Model NiCo concentrated solid solution alloys (specifically Co70Ni30, Co85Ni15, and Co90Ni10 compositions)
item.processing_route: Atomistic simulations using the Kim et al. Modified Embedded Atom Method potential; dislocations created via anisotropic displacement-field solution in simulation cells of 27,213,840 atoms; thermalized at 78 K and 850 K using Nose–Hoover thermostat under NVT conditions; energy minimization via conjugate gradient algorithm; decorrelation stress calculated by incrementally increasing target shear stress (σyz) by 40 MPa.
item.test_conditions: Temperatures of 78 K and 850 K; zero external stress for dissociation equilibrium; shear stress applied for decorrelation force measurements; simulation box length Lx = 1100 Å; dislocation line lengths varied from 69 to 1195 Å.
key_findings: Equilibrium separation distances remained finite for alloys with positive SFE (57.3 Å), zero SFE (84.9 Å), and negative SFE (109.5 Å) at 78 K, contrary to theoretical expectations for zero/negative SFE.
The average SFE values at 78 K were 19.8 mJ/m² for Co70Ni30, -0.8 mJ/m² for Co85Ni15, and -7.4 mJ/m² for Co90Ni10.
The standard deviation of local SFE values was 24.0 mJ/m² for Co70Ni30, 19.4 mJ/m² for Co85Ni15, and 17.5 mJ/m² for Co90Ni10.
The decorrelation force in zero and negative SFE alloys exceeded the upper bound of the local SFE distribution, indicating an additional resisting force.
The decorrelation force in the negative SFE alloy (Co90Ni10) was equal to the solute/dislocation interaction force (Fs), and nearly equal in the zero SFE alloy.
Direct solute–dislocation interaction energy predictions for the resisting force ranged from 17 to 30 mJ/m², whereas the reduced elastic interaction model predicted only 0.8–1.3 mJ/m².
The equilibrium separation distance in the positive SFE alloy coincided with the intersection of elastic force and the maximum SFE value, but not in the zero/negative SFE cases.
item.mechanism: In concentrated alloys, the SFE is not a unique value but a distribution; furthermore, the interaction of partial dislocations with the local solute environment creates a significant resisting force (Fs) due to solute/dislocation core interactions. The equilibrium dissociation distance is determined by the balance between the elastic repulsive force and the maximum of either the upper bound of the SFE distribution or the solute interaction force, rather than just the average SFE.
item.limitations: The study uses a model NiCo system which is not prone to short-range order (SRO) formation, meaning SRO contributions are not included in the force balance equation for this specific system.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that in real alloys with a tendency for SRO formation, the SRO contribution should be added to the force balance equation, and that other sources of resistance might be present in application to real alloys.
quotes: We use atomistic simulations in a model NiCo alloy to study the dislocation dissociation process in a range of compositions with positive, zero, and negative average SFE and surprisingly observe a stable, finite splitting distance in all cases at low temperatures.

Here, we show that the presence of a high solute/dislocation interaction, which is not easy to measure and neglected in experimental measurements of SFE, renders the experimental values of SFE unreliable.
